## Setting and question

In 2014 the Affordable Care Act offered states the option of expanding Medicaid to adults
under 138% of the federal poverty line, and opened the Marketplace for subsidised private
insurance. Medicaid spending rose in expansion states with the new enrollment.

We test whether Medicaid expansion displaced population-level spending, utilization or coverage by other payers in the same state. 

## Data and design

IHME Disease Expenditure Project (DEX 2.0): state-level spending and encounters by payer
and setting, all ages, 2010--2018, fit to SHEA state expenditure.
Uninsurance from CPS. **25 states** expanded on 1 January 2014;
the **19** that never expanded serve as controls. Later expanding
cohorts are dropped (n ≤ 3 per year).

Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) group-time difference-in-differences against the
never-expanded states, conditioning on covariates $X$: poverty rate, median household
income, pre-expansion uninsurance, and the shares under 18 and over 65:

```{=typst}
#block(width: 100%, above: 6mm, below: 6mm)[#set text(size: 26pt)
$ Delta Y_t = Y_t - Y_2013 $
$ "ATT"(t) = bb(E) [Delta Y_t | D=1] - bb(E) [bb(E) [Delta Y_t | X, D=0] | D=1] $]
```

Figures plot $\mathrm{ATT}(t)$; tables report the 2014--2018 average. **Inference** is a
multiplier bootstrap, 1,000 draws, clustered on state. **Parallel trends** is a Wald test
of $\mathrm{ATT}(t)=0$ across the three pre-expansion placebo years, $\chi^2_3$ on the
analytic clustered variance. **Multiplicity** is Benjamini--Hochberg across the 77
estimates in panel 4.

## 1. Expansion covered the uninsured

```{=typst}
#align(center, image("figures/f1_coverage.png", width: 82%))
```

| Coverage | Effect | 95% CI | Pre-test |
|:---------|-------:|:-------|---------:|
| Medicaid  | +3.69 | [+2.27, +5.12] | 0.84 |
| Medicare  | −0.20 | [−0.54, +0.14] | 0.72 |
| Uninsured | −1.38 | [−2.48, −0.28] | 0.30 |
| Private   | −2.16 | [−3.07, −1.24] | 0.96 |

Medicaid coverage rose **3.7 points** more in expansion states, and the uninsured rate
fell a further **1.4 points**. Private coverage grew in both groups, 62.9 to 64.4% in
expanders and 62.6 to 66.5% in controls.

```{=typst}
#colbreak()
```
### 2. New Medicaid enrollees had similar healthcare consumption

![](figures/f2_medicaid.png)

```{=typst}
#note[Difference-in-differences effect at each year relative to 2014, as a percentage of the pre-expansion level in expansion states. 95% intervals from multiplier bootstrap.]
```

Spending across expansion states rose **18.0%** (SE 3.9) after expansion alongside **19.9%**
increased enrollment, an additional **$189 per resident per year** on a pre-expansion base
of $1,051. Spending per enrollee was not affected: **−3.3%** (SE 4.4).

### 3. No significant change in private spending

![](figures/f3_private.png)

Private spending shows a small and non-significant increase in spend after expansion: 
**+4.8%** (SE 2.8) measured per enrollee and **+1.7%** (SE 2.4) per resident. 
These results do not show a compositional difference in new Marketplace enrollees 
between expansion and non-expansion states.


```{=typst}
#colbreak()
```
## 4. No effect outside Medicaid

We find no significant effect of the 2014 expansion on spending or encounters, per
resident or per enrollee, in any setting, for any payer other than Medicaid. Null estimates
are very precise for Medicare and for inpatient, emergency and ambulatory types of care. 
Imprecision is higher for out-of-pocket estimates and nursing and pharmacy care.

## Limitations

Estimates apply to the 2014 cohort and the never-expanded states through 2018. Impacts 
on late-expanding states, and long-term impacts after 2018 are not measured.

**Out-of-pocket reflects multiple types of payment.** DEX combines cost-sharing by the insured with all
spending by the uninsured, so compositional changes .

Population-level coverage and healthcare consumption data from DEX cannot identify individual
switching behavior across insurance types.
